title: Levodopa for Parkinson's
description: Levodopa is the main medicine for Parkinson's disease: the brain turns it into dopamine, replacing what is lost. One study scanned people in the early stage of Parkinson's, who had never taken the medicine, while they tapped their fingers, before and after a single dose. Before the dose, the motor cortex and the supplementary motor area were less active than in people without Parkinson's; after it, both became more active and movement improved. In the first part, brightness shows the difference from people without Parkinson's; in "What changed" it shows the change since before the dose.
caveat: All findings come from one study of 8 people with early Parkinson's affecting one side of the body, and 10 people without it. The effect of a single dose was measured over the following hour or so, not long-term treatment. The motor cortex finding is on the side opposite the affected hand; which side that is differed between people, so both sides are drawn. The authors note the supplementary motor area finding agrees with earlier studies, while the motor cortex finding has been controversial. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.

phases.name: Before treatment
phases.caption: Before the dose, while tapping fingers, the motor cortex and the supplementary motor area are less active than in people without Parkinson's.

phases.name: One dose of levodopa
phases.caption: A single dose of levodopa, then repeated scans every 20 minutes. The brain is drawn at rest here.

citations.authors: Buhmann C, Glauche V, Stürenburg HJ, Oechsner M, Weiller C, Büchel C
citations.title: Pharmacologically modulated fMRI--cortical responsiveness to levodopa in drug-naive hemiparkinsonian patients.
citations.quote: Patients performed a simple, auditory-paced random finger- opposition task every 3 s before and repeatedly every 20 min after intake of 300 mg of fast-release L-dopa.

phases.name: What changed
phases.caption: After the dose, the motor cortex and the supplementary motor area are more active during the same finger task, and movement is better. The two went closely together.

phases.name: What stayed the same
phases.caption: This shows a single dose in early Parkinson's. Over years, Parkinson's continues to progress, and the medicine's effect wears off between doses; that was not part of this study.

order.rationale: This last part is a summary of what the studies did not find or did not measure, not a later point in time.

regions.explanation: Less active than in people without Parkinson's before the dose, and more active after it, mainly on the side opposite the affected hand, in one study of 8 people. The authors note that this reversal was already established by earlier studies.
